title: Reserve-currency demand provides U.S. borrowing capacity whose loss would redistribute fiscal and household room
source_unit: NBER Working Paper 35328 and its nontechnical summary; general-equilibrium model calibrated with Federal Reserve Flow of Funds, trade, and convenience-yield evidence
geography: United States and global dollar-asset holders; modeled loss of U.S. reserve-currency status

observations.period: Observed context through 2025; NBER model issued June 2026

denominator.unit: foreign holdings and U.S. dollar public/private safe-asset markets; exact source-specific denominators vary

foreign_public_debt_share.value: roughly 45% to roughly 30% over the last two decades
foreign_public_debt_share.unit: share of U.S. public debt held by foreign investors

modeled_dollar_depreciation.unit: percent real depreciation under complete reserve-status loss in baseline calibration

modeled_real_rate_increase.unit: percentage points under complete reserve-status loss

modeled_foreign_bond_reabsorption.unit: percent of GDP in dollar bonds domestic investors would absorb in the model

modeled_wealth_loss.value: roughly one year of U.S. GDP, or about $18 trillion in the summary's calibration

observations.method: General-equilibrium model of goods and asset markets calibrated with U.S. Flow of Funds, foreign ownership of dollar assets, trade elasticities, home bias, and convenience-yield estimates.
observations.uncertainty: The modeled outcomes describe a counterfactual complete loss of reserve status, not a forecast or observed current loss. Results depend on calibration, substitution elasticities, home bias, asset demand, fiscal/monetary response, and the path of adjustment. Foreign-ownership decline and convenience-yield indicators do not by themselves establish reserve-status loss.
observations.subgroup: U.S. households, domestic investors, foreign dollar-asset holders, Treasury and financial markets, and sectors exposed to exchange-rate and interest-rate adjustment; distribution within each group is not modeled in this record.
observations.counterinterpretation: Reserve demand can change without a discrete loss of status; dollar private-asset demand, safe-asset supply, policy credibility, and geopolitical alternatives may move differently. A real depreciation can benefit exporters while raising import costs, and aggregate wealth loss does not identify household incidence or policy response.

related_sources.claim: NBER summary separates foreign-ownership context, convenience yield, model calibration, and counterfactual reserve-status consequences.

boundary: This record adds a reserve-demand-to-state-capacity pathway. It does not establish that the United States has lost reserve status, predict a future depreciation or rate increase, or show distributional household, firm, political, or geopolitical outcomes from such a change.
